newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU monetary committee meets on EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU monetary committee meets on EMU.

text.p: The European Union's monetary committee met on Tuesday to work on the technical details of economic and monetary union (EMU), in particular the legal text for a budget stability pact, sources said.
The committee is expected to assess the results of a summit of EU leaders in Dublin last month where agreement was reached on a number of important issues, including the stability pact.
"The stability pact has to be converted into a legal text," said one source familiar with the committee's deliberations.

While that procedure is not expected to pose any substantial problems, officials said there was a need to spell out more precisely the effect the pact would have on the economic convergence programs of those not qualifying for EMU in 1999.
The agreed pact would fine governments running deficits above three percent of total output. It also lays out the economic conditions under which governments could avoid sanctions.

Much of the committee's work over the next six months is expected to be of a technical nature and therefore devoid of the high political drama that accompanied the debate over the stability pact last year.

As an example, officials pointed to the issue of countries not qualifying for monetary union at the start date. An important question is whether they should be let in immediately after meeting the Maastricht treaty's criteria or after a suitable delay.

"What happens if Italy qualifies in March of 1999," asked one official. "There might be a desire to allow the euro (the single currency) to get on its feet and keep any new qualifiers on hold for the moment."

Other areas of concern include the changeover of public administrations. How rapidly governments convert their accounting and tax systems into the euro will influence the speed by which the single currency is used in the private sector, say officials.

There will also be more talk on the external value of the euro, particularly against the dollar, as well as debate over the conversion rates that will be used to lock national currencies to the single currency.
